title: Relative Sort Array
description: Sort one array to match another array's relative order, with unlisted elements appended in ascending order, using a rank-lookup comparator.

blocks.text: Given arr1 and arr2 (arr2 has distinct elements, all present in arr1, arr1 may have duplicates), sort arr1 so elements appear in the same relative order as arr2. Elements not present in arr2 should be appended at the end, sorted in ascending order.

blocks.caption: Mapping each arr2 value to its position gives a sort key covering both listed and unlisted elements.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","arr1[] (may have duplicates), arr2[] (distinct, all present in arr1)"],["Output","arr1 sorted by arr2's order first, then unlisted elements ascending"]]}

blocks.text: Sorting by a CUSTOM priority order (defined by another array) rather than natural numeric order is a custom-comparator sorting problem: build a lookup from value to its priority rank, then sort using that rank as the key, with a sensible fallback rank for values outside the priority list.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: The "map to a rank, then sort by that rank" technique reapplies whenever an external ordering (not the values themselves) determines the sort order.

Picture arr2 as a priority list handed out in advance. Every item in arr1 that appears on this priority list gets grouped and ordered exactly as the list specifies. Anything not on the list is placed at the very end, sorted normally among themselves.

blocks.caption: Priority-listed items come first in their specified order; everything else follows, sorted normally.

items: Build a map from each arr2 value to its index (its priority rank).
Sort arr1 using that rank as the primary key; assign an "infinite" rank (larger than any real rank) to values not in arr2.
For values sharing the same fallback (not-in-arr2) rank, break ties by their natural value, ascending.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Value","Rank (or fallback)"],"rows":[["2","0"],["1","1"],["4","2"],["3","3"],["9","4"],["6","5"],["7 (not in arr2)","fallback, sorted by value"],["19 (not in arr2)","fallback, sorted by value"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Sorting by rank produces [2,2,2,1,4,3,3,9,6,7,19], matching the expected output. 7 and 19 (both not in arr2) fall after everything else, in ascending order.
A direct approach scans arr1 once per arr2 value, collecting matches in order, then separately collects and sorts the leftovers. This is correct but does an O(n) scan for every value in arr2.
Building a rank lookup once, then sorting arr1 directly with a comparator using that rank, achieves the same result in a single efficient sort, without needing repeated linear scans.
For each value in arr2 (in order), scan arr1 collecting all matching unused elements. Then collect and sort the remaining unmatched elements.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n * m)","n = arr1 length, m = arr2 length, each arr2 value scans all of arr1"],["Space","O(n)","The result and remaining arrays"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Scanning all of arr1 for every arr2 value is unnecessary once a rank lookup can answer "where does this value belong" in O(1).

Build a hash map from each arr2 value to its index. Sort arr1 directly using a comparator: values in the map use their rank; values not in the map use a fallback rank (larger than any real rank), with ties among fallback values broken by natural ascending order.

items: Build the rank map from arr2, O(m).
Sort arr1 with a comparator using that map, O(n log n).
Values not in the map naturally sort after all ranked values and among themselves in ascending order.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, scan arr1 per arr2 value","O(n * m)","O(n)"],["Optimized, rank map + custom sort","O(n log n + m)","O(n)"]]}

items: Sorting by an external, pre-defined order is done by mapping values to a rank, then sorting by that rank.
A large fallback rank cleanly pushes unlisted values to the end without special-casing them separately.
This rank-lookup-then-sort pattern generalizes to any "custom priority order" sorting requirement.

blocks.text: Relative Sort Array is solved by mapping each value in arr2 to its index (its priority rank), then sorting arr1 with a comparator using that rank, falling back to natural ascending order (with a rank larger than any listed value) for elements not in arr2, giving an O(n log n) solution.
